summary:
PaddyField Shift is an innovative decision-support framework developed by Team USM Kejuruteraan for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to optimize off-season crop rotation in Malaysian paddy granaries.  
​
The project established a multi-sensor analytics framework and interactive prototype that synthesizes NASA Earth observations—specifically SMAP for soil moisture, ECOSTRESS for land-surface temperature, and GPM/IMERG for precipitation tracking—alongside ESA Sentinel-2, JAXA ALOS-2, and local MADA schedules. It translates these telemetry streams into actionable microclimate risk zones and evaluates three management pathways: continuous monoculture, post-harvest legume cover crops (Strategy A), and deep-rooting crop rotation (Strategy B).  
​
It addresses the "Field Shift" challenge by turning open-source orbital data into localized agricultural intelligence. By matching environmental stress indicators to specific crop functional traits, the system guides farmers away from depleting monocultures toward restorative rotation strategies.  
​
It provides smallholder farmers with practical, evidence-based guidance to restore soil fertility, reverse subsurface compaction, improve water infiltration, and build long-term resilience against extreme climate shocks.
details:
Project Details: PaddyField Shift


​1. What does it do and how does it work?


PaddyField Shift is an interactive geospatial decision-support dashboard designed to help Malaysian paddy farmers transition from continuous rice monoculture to climate-resilient crop rotations. The system ingests and synthesizes multi-sensor NASA Earth observation datasets—specifically SMAP for surface and root-zone soil moisture, ECOSTRESS for land-surface temperature (LST) and evapotranspiration, and GPM/IMERG for rainfall accumulation and monsoon anomalies—alongside ESA Sentinel-2 optical vegetation indices and JAXA ALOS-2 land-cover data. Using these telemetry streams, the dashboard calculates a composite Field Risk Score (categorizing parcels into Green, Amber, or Red intervention zones) and recommends tailored off-season rotation strategies: Strategy A (post-harvest nitrogen-fixing legume cover crops) or Strategy B (deep-rooting crops to fracture compacted soil layers).

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Reverses Soil Degradation: Restores natural soil nitrogen pools and breaks up hard subsurface plow pans caused by continuous wet rice cultivation.
  • Water & Fertilizer Optimization: Reduces dependency on expensive synthetic urea fertilizers and optimizes freshwater retention during erratic dry spells.
  • Data-Driven Certainty: Eliminates guesswork for smallholder farmers by translating complex orbital satellite measurements into simple, actionable field-level advisories.
  • Supplementary Farm Income: Enables farmers to cultivate profitable, short-cycle off-season rotation crops (such as mung beans, groundnuts, or sweet potatoes) during fallow intervals.


​3. What is the intended impact of the project?


PaddyField Shift aims to safeguard national food security and protect rural smallholder livelihoods across major Malaysian granary regions such as the Muda Agricultural Development Authority (MADA) area in Kedah. By operationalizing open-source NASA Earth science data at the grassroots level, the project empowers farmers and agricultural extension agencies to build long-term agro-ecosystem resilience against monsoon variability, heat stress, and soil exhaustion while minimizing agricultural chemical runoff into surrounding river basins.


​4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop the project?

  • AI & Rapid Coding Environment: We utilized Google AI Studio (powered by Gemini models) to generate, structure, and refine the frontend dashboard code, interactive UI components, and agronomic decision-tree logic.
  • Web & Analytical Technologies: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and Python (for satellite data normalization, agronomic benchmark modeling, and visualization charts).
  • NASA & Partner Open Data Sources: NASA Earthdata (SMAP, ECOSTRESS via AppEEARS, GPM/IMERG via GES DISC), Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem (ESA Sentinel-2), JAXA ALOS-2/PALSAR-2, and MADA regional planting schedules.
  • ​Hardware & Collaboration Tools: Standard engineering laptops for cloud-based coding and geospatial synthesis, alongside Canva and presentation tools for visual documentation.


​5. How is the project creative?


Instead of presenting raw, intimidating satellite maps or complex meteorological spreadsheets that non-technical users struggle to interpret, PaddyField Shift creatively bridges orbital remote sensing with practical biological engineering. It pairs specific satellite-detected environmental stresses (such as high thermal stress and subsurface compaction) directly with targeted plant root architectures ("bio-drilling" deep roots vs. nitrogen-fixing legumes), turning everyday crop selection into an automated soil-rehabilitation tool.

6. What factors did our team consider?

  • Tropical Cloud Cover Interference: Because Peninsular Malaysia experiences persistent equatorial cloud cover that blocks optical satellites, our team anchored core soil and rainfall diagnostics on cloud-penetrating microwave sensors (SMAP and GPM).
  • Smallholder Plot Fragmentation: Malaysian paddy lots are typically small (1–3 hectares). We integrated higher-resolution ECOSTRESS thermal data (70 m) and Sentinel-2 indices (10 m) to downscale broader soil moisture grids to practical farm levels.
  • ​Local Agronomic & Cultural Fit: All rotation recommendations were cross-checked against official MADA off-season fallow windows and local crop viability so recommendations remain realistic for Malaysian farmers.
  • ​Accessibility & Simplicity: The dashboard interface was designed with intuitive color-coded risk zones so farmers and local extension officers can make decisions quickly without needing geospatial training.
